analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income tax with a 15 percent national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 19, 1997 with 19 cosponsors (15 Republicans, 4 Democrats), the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the federal income tax, the estate tax, the gift tax, and most excise taxes, and replace them with a 15 percent tax on everything consumers buy, collected mostly by the states. It would shut down the IRS by cutting off its funding after fiscal year 2001 and let the Social Security Administration handle payroll taxes instead. To soften the blow on the poor, it includes a 'family consumption refund' that rebates the tax on spending up to the federal poverty level through paychecks. The bill never got any action after its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: they would pay no income tax, no capital gains tax, and no estate or gift tax, and would be taxed only on what they spend. Businesses gain by having their income tax eliminated and all purchases for business purposes exempted from the sales tax. Low-income families get partial protection through the poverty-level rebate, but working and middle-class families who spend most of what they earn would bear a new 15 percent tax on nearly every purchase, stacked on top of existing state sales taxes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, estate and gift taxes, and most excise taxes, replacing them with a single 15 percent tax on consumption [S2][S3].
Exempts all purchases made for a business purpose and all exports, so productive investment escapes the tax entirely [S2][S3].

Provides a family consumption refund that rebates the sales tax on spending up to the federal poverty level, delivered through paychecks and administered by the Social Security Administration [S2][S3].

Phases out the IRS by prohibiting appropriations after fiscal year 2001 and shifts collection to states, which keep a 1 percent administration fee, with a new Treasury Sales Tax Bureau for non-conforming states [S2][S3].
Allows homebuyers to pay the tax on a principal residence in installments over 30 years, and requires a supermajority in each chamber to raise the tax rate [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Working and middle-class families bear the main cost: because they spend nearly all of their income, a 15 percent tax on consumption takes a much larger share of their earnings than of high earners', who can save and invest tax-free. The poverty-level rebate shields only spending up to the poverty line. Consumers also face the tax on financial services fees and on new-home purchases (unless spread over 30 years), and the bill removes the progressive income tax and estate tax that currently fall most heavily on the wealthiest households.
analysis.who_pays_short: Working families who spend most of their income

drawbacks.text: A consumption tax is regressive by design: a family spending its entire paycheck pays the tax on 15 percent of its income, while a wealthy household living off accumulated savings pays almost nothing, and the rebate only offsets tax on spending up to the poverty level [S3].

Repealing the estate and gift taxes and exempting savings, investment returns, and business purchases means the entire burden of funding the federal government shifts from wealth and capital onto current consumption, which is dominated by wage earners [S2][S3].

States would have to rewrite their own sales taxes to conform to the federal tax's definitions, exemptions, and credits or lose the right to collect the federal tax, and the federal government could take over collection only after a state court ruling [S3].

Taxing 'implicit' financial intermediation income (the spread between lending and deposit rates) is administratively novel and would subject banks, insurers, and brokerages to a levy they do not pay under the income tax [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real simplification — ending income tax filing for households and businesses — and genuinely protects the poorest families through the rebate. But the core trade is regressive: it swaps a tax graded by ability to pay for a tax graded by spending, and simultaneously eliminates the estate tax and taxes on investment gains, which concentrates the benefit on the wealthiest households. Whether 15 percent would actually fund the government at current levels was widely disputed; if not, the rate would have to rise, worsening the regressivity. It is a large, permanent transfer of tax burden from wealth to wages.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Schaefer of Colorado introduced the National Retail Sales Tax Act of 1997 on June 19, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5][S1].
Nineteen members cosponsored the bill: 15 Republicans and 4 Democrats [S4].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing income tax system, and the industries and households that do well under it, stayed exactly as they were: no tax burden shifted from wealth to wages, and the tax preparation, accounting, and software businesses built on the income tax kept their market. Wealthy households continued to pay income and estate taxes that the bill would have repealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing income tax system and tax-prep industry

for.name: Rep. Dan Schaefer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Retail Sales Tax Act of 1997 and recruited 19 cosponsors for it

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was mostly Republican — 15 of the 19 cosponsors were Republicans, though 4 Democrats joined — and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never moved the bill, so the fight never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill eliminates income tax on investment returns, capital gains, and estates — taxes that fall almost entirely on the top of the income distribution — and replaces the revenue with a tax on consumption, which takes a far larger share of a working family's income than of a wealthy one's.

industries.industry: Tax preparation, accounting, and tax software
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and abolishing the IRS would eliminate the annual filing burden that this industry is built to serve. Ordinary taxpayers who currently pay for preparation would be relieved of that cost.

Retailers would have to register, collect, report, and remit a 15 percent federal tax on top of state sales taxes (with a compliance equipment credit and an administration credit), but all business-purpose purchases are exempt and the tax is simply passed through to customers in higher prices.

The bill imposes a 15 percent tax on explicitly charged financial fees and on 'implicit' intermediation income such as the deposit-lending spread — a levy that does not exist under current law — but financial services used in business and the first $10,000 of fees are exempt, and costs would likely flow to customers through higher fees.
The bill taxes gross gaming receipts (less payoffs) at 15 percent, a cost casinos and other gaming operators would pass on to players through worse odds or higher prices.

industries.industry: State governments with conforming sales taxes
industries.note: States that conform their sales tax rules to the federal tax would collect the federal tax and keep a 1 percent administration fee, giving their tax agencies new revenue and staffing.
